#7516. YouTube enlists educational creators to show the value of its interactive gaming hub

As educators, researchers, and policymakers debate YouTube’s utility in classrooms, a handful of creators are getting the chance to show how the platform’s interactive elements can enhance learning. YouTube quietly introduced a slate of educational games through its Playables hub, with notable STEM channels like Veritasium and Khan Academy involved in the initiative.

Playables has been available on YouTube for nearly three years, but for much of its existence, the hub has been little more than a motley collection of low-stakes, casual titles. Though YouTube has tested some upgrades for its gaming destination, the reach and influence of Playables pale in comparison to YouTube’s traditional video library.

Last week, YouTube showed that Playables could have significant potential in scholastic settings. With its six-game library of educational titles, YouTube is helping players learn about subjects like physics, economics, and music theory within fun, interactive settings.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Veritasium’s contribution to the new gaming library is Elements of Truth, a simple trivia challenge that tests players’ scientific knowledge. According to Luke Lewis, the Director of Publishing at Electrify Video Partners — which invested in Veritasium in 2023 — YouTube came calling earlier this year to propose Playables tie-ins for Electrify’s brands. Lewis told Tubefilter that Electrify saw the proposal as an opportunity to promote Veritasium’s Elements of Truth tabletop game.

“Our long-term expectations are for the game to introduce Elements of Truth to an audience of knowledge-hungry casual gamers who might otherwise not be familiar with it – and in fact might not even be familiar with Veritasium‘s videos,” Lewis said. “At the same time, we hope it will deepen engagement among existing Veritasium fans, encourage them to get competitive with fellow fans, and have fun doing it.”

Lewis said that the initial response to the Playables title has been “extremely positive.” Orders for the physical Elements of Truth game have spiked as Veritasium fans have shared their Playables high scores with each other.

As useful as Playables has been for Electrify and Veritasium, it might be even more valuable for YouTube itself. Though the platform has thrown resources behind educational initiatives led by top creators, it has also faced ban threats in schools, most notably in the New York City school district. Detractors may argue that a platform like YouTube can only be a distraction in the classroom, but games like Elements of Truth suggest otherwise.

In previous years, interactive games on YouTube have been the domain of marketing agencies and tech-savvy tinkerers. Perhaps, given the positive response Electrify has seen, we’re about to enter into an era of good-for-you games on Google’s video platform. YouTube is certainly committed to promoting Playables. It recently introduced accessability tags that help users find the games that best fit their device’s settings. So if you want to try to beat my Elements of Truth high score (which won’t be too hard), finding and playing the game should be a cinch.

#7513. How The Athletic Gets More Clicks With One Simple Trick

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

The Athletic uses comment counts to highlight its most discussion-worthy content. It's something more publishers should experiment with.

Getting people to click on articles is becoming increasingly difficult. We’ve been lazily conditioned by big tech’s greed, and it shows no sign of slowing.

To combat this, we have to build and own audiences and get better at marketing. Publishers need to work harder to make their content appealing, particularly on the surfaces they control.

The Athletic does something very simple on its homepage that more publishers should consider: It shows readers how many comments selected articles have generated.

It tells you which content its readers really care about.

Now part of the world’s most successful publisher, The Athletic has gone from strength to strength in recent times. In Q2 of 2025, revenue was up one-third to $54 million with an adjusted operating profit of $5.8 million. Hell, even ad revenue nearly doubled to $14.1 million.

Safe to say The New York Times, and by extension The Athletic, are publishing’s most profitable case study. They are worth listening to.

It tells you, dear apathetic reader, which articles are generating discussion. It’s an extremely simple, clever use of social proof.

Depending on the importance you place on comments and engagement, this can be foundational to your on-site distribution strategy. (Image Credit: Harry Clarkson-Bennett)

People are naturally drawn to things other people are interested in. And every publisher is trying to create a community. These comment counts signal which articles are generating discussion among its audience. Arguably other like-minded people.

If one article has 500 comments and another has just one, all things being equal, I’m far more likely to click on the former. It has piqued my curiosity. Clickability goes beyond just images and headlines.

It tells me there’s a conversation worth joining. Or, at the very least, something interesting enough to get people talking.

This is particularly valuable if you have a large homepage and direct audience. As traffic continues to drop, you’ve got to make more use of what you have.

Comments are just one measure of engagement. We can be far more rigorous.

Experiment with shares, likes, and other signals to identify content that resonates with your audience. Tell your audience, with certainty, which articles are worth reading.

Not every article will generate hundreds of comments, even the more popular ones. Some might be widely shared, others might encourage unusually high levels of engagement relative to your traffic.

The important thing is identifying what your audience values and making that visible. That you prioritize your best-performing content.

Most publishers use composite engagement scores to promote the right behaviors. Almost everyone is de-prioritizing traffic and promoting quality engagement – session duration, clicks, scroll depth, comments – because they believe this is the key to building a truly engaged audience.

You could use statistical modeling, potentially supported by AI, to identify articles that are over-performing against expected engagement levels (a Bayesian like approach), then surface them more prominently across homepages, section fronts and topic pages.

Rather than relying exclusively on editorial judgement, you’re combining it with actual audience behavior.

The result should be a better user experience and more opportunities to generate clicks.

Keep it really, really simple and set clear key performance indicators.

CTR is not a perfect measure of success. Often, the most clickable content can veer into rage-bait or clickbait. Which is exactly the kind of content you want to avoid.

As referral traffic becomes harder to generate, publishers need to make more of the audiences they already have. This is a simple, almost certainly effective way of doing that.

SEO Director at The Telegraph with a decade of experience. Unskilled jiu-jitsu guy. Average chess player. Jack of many things.

#7508. Top 5 Branded Videos of the Week: The adrenaline spectrum

Welcome to our rundown of the most-watched branded YouTube videos of the week.

We’re publishing this snippet of a larger Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report in order to analyze sponsorship trends in the creator economy. Any video launched in tandem with an official brand partner is eligible for t he ranking.

And–as the name up above would imply–all the data comes from Gospel Stats. If you’re interested in learning more about Gospel–and which brands are sponsoring what creators on YouTube–click here. You can also download our YouTube 2025 Sponsorship Landscape Report here.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

This week’s Gospel Stats Brand Report kicks off with an adrenaline rush and then tapers into a nice relaxing day trip to the lake. In between, we’ve got a YouTube-sponsored video, some questionable fitness decisions, and more.

#1 If You Escape, You Win $1,000,000 Channel: MrBeast Gaming and Call of Duty Brand: Call of Duty Views: 56,792,187

Something something we got MrBeast in Call of Duty before GTA 6.

There’s $1 million on the line in Jimmy Beast’s new collab with CoD promotes its latest Modern Warfare installment–and specifically the game’s “DMZ” mode, which pits players against each other and the environment around them. With NPC dangers lurking, players can choose to team up for safety in numbers…but eventually all bonds must break, as only one team can emerge victorious.

MrBeast’s video drops 10 teams into a real-life army camp where they split into their own technologically tricked out tents and hop into a DMZ match. The last team alive in-game keeps the cash prize IRL.

MrBeast called this collab a “dream come true,” and we’re guessing CoD‘s developers might feel similarly, considering the view count for this video. They also produced a Short together this week; that one came in at #9 on our list, with more than 12 million views.

#2 I cant stop listening to the song ? @YouTube #YouTubePartner #sofimanassyan #LISA Channel: Sofi Manassyan Brand: YouTube Views: 26,314,085

Blackpink‘s YouTube dominance might never fade. Its frontwoman dancer and rapper, LISA, is square in the spotlight for this new YouTube-sponsored promo.

Manyassan doesn’t mention her sponsor till the last couple seconds of the video, where, through faux fan tears, she tells viewers to go watch more LISA content on YouTube.

This is an intriguing one for us. YouTube has historically rarely sponsored creators–but in the past couple years, it’s brought groups of creators to major events like the World Cup, teamed up with Mark Rober for his STEM education initiative, and signed a multiyear partnership with MrBeast that spans numerous Google products. (There’s also the thing with it paying creators to stay off Netflix.)

And, on top of its creator team-ups, YouTube has been pushing its Music service, one of the key areas where it competes with other platforms like Spotify. Combining the two might be some pretty strong sauce.

#3 I Survived Chinas Fat Loss Prison Channel: Browney Brand: Gymshark, Myprotein Views: 18,223,893

MrBeast isn’t the only channel hitting our top 5 with a weight loss challenge video. The difference is, Browney himself is the one in the hot seat.

He went to China and sent himself to one of the country’s “fat loss prisons,” where people who want to lose weight voluntarily (at least, it’s supposed to be voluntary) enter and are not allowed to leave until they’ve gotten skinnier. While they’re in the “prison,” people sleep in dorms, do four hours of exercise a day, and have strictly controlled meals.

Browney, whose YouTube tagline is “everything is a challenge,” spends 50 hours in the place getting to know his fellow “inmates,” hearing their stories, and experiencing what they’re going through to lose weight. Perhaps unsurprisingly, his upload is sponsored by two fitness brands: workout clothing company Gymshark and supplement company Myprotein.

#4 Riding 1300 Miles to Alaska on Jet Ski – Camping & Fishing Channel: Matt Spears Brand: AnyDesk Views: 17,221,584

This two-hour odyssey of a video chronicles creator Matt Spears‘ much longer odyssey. He recently became the first person to jetski up the West Coast of the U.S., along the shores of Canada, and up to Alaska. It was an enormous undertaking: 1,300 miles of near-constant travel, all his gear and fuel packed into one vehicle, and nobody to rely on but himself.

His accomplishment has racked up more than 17 million views for his sponsor AnyDesk, and is part of the company’s overall creator support initiative.

“If you have any ridiculous experiments that you would love to see your favorite YouTubers test online you can submit them here. If you submit an idea that ends up being used for a video we will ship you some swag and potentially a prop from one of the videos,” AnyDesk–which makes remote desktop software–said on a landing page linked by Spears. “At AnyDesk, we’re passionate about science, creativity, and collaboration. Whether it’s testing a car battery-powered computer or building something completely ridiculous, we love connecting people who think outside the box.”

AnyDesk also sponsored two other videos this week: #537 from Scammer Payback, and #944 from Trilogy Media.

BONUS #5,029 autumn in los angeles | unique coffee recipes, lake arrowhead day trip Channel: Brandon Chou Brand: Away Views: 43,527

So much of our YouTube feeds these days are ultra-high-energy shoutfests, super-tuned to keep viewers glued as long as possible. It can feel like a treat when something comes up and no one’s yelling at you or going Taken with the editing.

Slow and easy is the vibe with Brandon Chou‘s week-in-the-life vlog, where he leaves L.A. behind and takes viewers up to Lake Arrowhead, which is nestled in the San Bernardino National Forest at 5,000 feet elevation. Being that close to the sky means lots of great shots, and Chou lingers on them as he and his friends walk through the local shops, pick up ingredients to make dinner in their Airbnb, and roast marshmallows to the sound of lapping water.

The video is, fittingly, sponsored by luggage company Away, and though Chou’s plug for the company is relatively short, his entire vlog lures viewers with a call-to-action, telling them: get out of the city, away from the stress, and go look at something beautiful.

…and there’s a lot more data where that came from. If you like our Weekly Top 5, you’ll love everything else Gospel has to offer.

seoClarity's Chris Sachs and Aris Vrakas explained how readable pages, shopper language, consistent product feeds, and testing support AI shopping discovery.

A product can have the right material, price, and features and still give an AI shopping tool too little context to recommend it. The challenge is not simply getting a feed accepted. It is making product information retrievable, relevant to shopper needs, and consistent wherever it appears.

In this webinar, AI Shopping: Get Your Products Found In Google & ChatGPT, Chris Sachs, VP of Value Enablement, and Aris Vrakas, Product Lead at seoClarity, walked through four connected moves: make product pages readable, enrich content in shopper language, synchronize feeds and pages, and measure what changed.

The session focused on work ecommerce teams could do now, rather than waiting for checkout inside AI services to mature.

Vrakas began with a technical prerequisite: product content needed to be available to bots, not only visible to someone using a browser. He described JavaScript-heavy pages where shoppers could see details that an automated fetch did not expose.

For teams reviewing their stores, that distinction calls for checking what a crawler actually receives. Are core product details present in the HTML? Does important information depend on client-side execution? Where rendering was a bottleneck, Vrakas discussed prerendering and cached HTML as options.

His point was to address access before investing heavily in enrichment. Better descriptions cannot help a system that never receives them.

The presenters used socks as a recurring example. Color and fiber composition are useful attributes, but they do not answer every question about warmth, thickness, durability, or intended use. Vrakas explained that conversational prompts could combine several of those needs in one request.

He recommended connecting product characteristics with the decisions shoppers were trying to make. Rather than leaving an AI model to infer a use case from a short specification, retailers could provide relevant details directly. He also discussed using attributable review evidence to support claims about how a product performed.

The opportunity was not limited to unusually long prompts. Vrakas explained that even a broad request for a good product could lead an AI system to consider more specific attributes. The webinar’s product-enrichment discussion explored how retailers could anticipate those questions without relying on generic descriptions.

Sachs warned against treating the product feed as a separate project owned somewhere else in the organization. Information added to a feed should also inform the product page and its structured data, rather than stopping at the feed.

Vrakas described why that consistency mattered when a platform revisited a product page: product identity, price, and supporting details needed to be clear and coherent. An enriched feed did not remove the need to make the corresponding page understandable.

The presenters called this closing the loop. For an ecommerce team, it meant connecting SEO, merchandising, paid media, and development so that one channel’s improvements could benefit another, instead of maintaining disconnected versions of the same product information.

The presenters separated three areas of measurement:

These were different signals, not interchangeable definitions of success. An AI mention alone did not establish a sale, and the presenters encouraged teams to examine the effects across the channels they were changing.

Chris Sachs tied that measurement work to ongoing experimentation:

“The best SEO teams are the ones that obsess about testing. The more testing you do, the better decision making you can have.”

During the Q&A, a viewer asked whether a before-and-after comparison was enough to evaluate generative engine optimization. Vrakas distinguished large catalogs, where product groups could support comparisons, from smaller sites or broader brand questions. For the latter, he described improving content around a defined topic and comparing its movement with other topics left untouched.

The useful distinction was having a comparison set, rather than assuming that every visibility change proved an optimization had worked.

The full on-demand session connected technical retrieval, feed enrichment, and measurement examples. To turn the discussion into a first review with your team:

#7503. The code for YouTube’s Android app reveals a testing ground for Instagram-style social features

The most recent version of YouTube‘s Android app includes some curious lines of code. A report from Android Authority reveals numerous references to Tamba, a mysterious entity that has some similarities to Instagram.

Android Authority‘s discoveries within the YouTube app include the logo pictured above and dozens of icons that share a crude aesthetic reminiscent of hand-drawn images. Those assets are tied to a package titled “com.google.android.youtube.sandbox,” suggesting that Tamba is a separate experience from the primary version of YouTube.

Based on the use of the word “sandbox” in that string, one hypothesis is that Tamba is nothing more than an experimental platform used to test new features before they’re pushed to YouTube. But Android Authority notes that the code references a separate “test” package, which means that Tamba could be something more than a digital lab.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Some of the terms used in the Tamba assets sound more like what you’d expect to see on Instagram rather than YouTube. There are references to followers, direct messages, and group chats. Tamba’s chats may also be able to integrate formats from the main version of YouTube, including Shorts.

If YouTube is trying to develop its own take on Instagram, it wouldn’t be the first tech company to utilize that strategy. Meta’s perceived abandonment of the qualities that made O.G. Instagram so popular have opened up opportunities for rivals. The photo app Dispo, for example, enjoyed a brief surge by telling its users that it’s not Instagram. More recently, TikTok embraced different types of photo content as part of an effort to revive the bygone Instagram experience.

YouTube, for its part, has built up its DMs as Instagram has turned those messages into a revenue stream. DMs haven’t traditionally been a big part of YouTube’s approach to community, but if Tamba is a real thing, it could put that form of correspondance front and center.

Of course, that’s a big if. YouTube runs all sorts of tests all the time, and it’s important to accept that Tamba could ultimately amount to little. But Instagram is eager to encroach on YouTube’s territory by allowing long-form video uploads. It wouldn’t be a surprise if YouTube returned the favor.

TikTok is highlighting two impression share metrics for Search Ads and adding curated keyword packs. Here's what each does.

TikTok’s Product Preview of Q4 2026 shows two impression share metrics for Search Ads Campaigns, and TikTok is adding curated keyword groups called Keyword Packs to their Keyword Suggestion Tool.

The two share metrics are designed to measure how much of the eligible search inventory a campaign is taking advantage of, and TikTok’s guide to low shares begins by asking if the campaign has already exhausted its budget.

TikTok’s help page defines these metrics as follows:

Impression Share: The percentage of eligible search results impressions your ads captured.

Top 1 Impression Share: The percentage of eligible first-position search results impressions your ads captured.

The Oct. 30 post describes them in auction terms, as showing “the percentage of eligible search auctions an advertiser’s keywords successfully won on the Search Results Page.” Neither page explains how TikTok counts the eligible opportunities a campaign didn’t win.

The post says the metrics are available at the campaign, advertiser, and keyword levels in TikTok Ads Manager. The help page says Ads Manager may show them for eligible Search Ads Campaign and TopSearch campaigns. TopSearch, a CPM-billed Search Ads option, places an ad in the first sponsored position for a keyword when it wins the auction.

Availability can differ depending on your account, campaign type, market, and product rollout status, as noted on the help page.

According to TikTok’s Help Page, if a campaign has a low impression share, then based upon other factors (budget, bidding, keyword coverage, creative relevance, competition level, and/or fluctuation of search volume), there could be an opportunity to capture additional eligible impressions.

The troubleshooting section of the help page uses spending to distinguish between the first two. If a campaign spends all of its available money, the help page recommends increasing the campaign’s budget to see if you are able to capitalize on more eligible impressions. However, when a campaign does not spend its available funds, the help page recommends checking whether your bid is competitive for those same keywords. The rest of the suggestions include reviewing your keyword list for opportunities to add new ones as well as making sure that your creative and landing pages match your keywords.

Neither the Help Page nor the Reporting Guide published by TikTok in April provided information on metrics to measure how much of a campaign’s impression share was being lost due to budget or ranking.

TikTok says its Keyword Suggestion Tool “can now recommend” Keyword Packs to advertisers, “ready-made, curated” based on brand and category keywords. Advertisers can preview and add these suggested packs using the same workflow used today. In addition, according to TikTok, the pack suggestions are refreshed each day, utilizing metrics including (but not limited to) search volume, cost-per-click (CPC) and competition, allowing advertisers to utilize keyword lists “backed by TikTok’s machine learning models.”

Brooke Osmundson wrote about the inclusion of keyword suggestions within Search Ads setup when it first launched in the U.S. in September 2024. The current version of the help section, which was last revised in November 2025, does reference suggested keywords with monthly impression predictions and match types, but does so without referencing packs. Also, TikTok provides a different Keyword Planner, which contains information regarding search volume and competition for advertising planners wishing to develop their own keyword lists.

The post doesn’t say which markets or accounts can use Keyword Packs, or how TikTok chooses the terms in a brand pack.

Where a share metric appears in your TikTok account, go to the keyword-level view to find keywords getting only a small percentage of their eligible impressions. Once you have identified those terms, then proceed with checking if your campaign has fully exhausted its budget using TikTok’s troubleshooting steps.

For Keyword Packs, the preview TikTok describes is the place to review brand terms before adding them.

The October 30th post and TikTok’s Search Ads overview are the only areas I could locate on the site regarding Keyword Packs. TikTok’s suggestion tool help page, which was last updated in November 2025, will be an area to keep an eye on for market and account information as well. Until this page is updated, you can check Ads Manager to see if your account includes either of these features within reporting for Share Metrics and when setting up keywords for the Keyword Packs.

#7500. Midterm election traffic spiked on Twitch, but Hasan Piker can’t hold a candle to Steve Kornacki

The 2026 U.S. midterm elections resulted in a historic victory for Democrats, but liberals weren’t the only big winners on the night of November 3. Streamers across YouTube, Twitch, Kick, and Rumble picked up more viewership than they’ve ever received during midterm election coverage.

According to Streams Charts, election-related broadcasts on those four platforms combined to haul in 20.87 hours of watch time, collectively reaching 3.4 million concurrent viewers. Across 3,400 channels, election night traffic was more than four times higher than it was during the previous midterms in 2022. (Streams during the presidential election year of 2024, however, did deliver more traffic.)

The increasing midterms viewership on streaming platforms underscored creators’ growing influence in American politics. After Trump used his connections with creators to gain ground in 2024, Democrats fought back by forging their own alliances. Several of the biggest winners in 2026 — including Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, and Texas Senator-elect James Talarico — boosted their campaigns through robust social media strategies.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The results of that push can be seen on Streams Charts‘ list of the most-watched midterms broadcasts of 2026. Progressive lightning rod Hasan Piker attracted 1.75 million hours of watch time on his November 3 Twitch stream. On the right side of the aisle, Steven Crowder made a big impression on Rumble, bringing in 461,000 hours of watch time.

One of the U.S. Congressional reps who has recognized the political power of creators is California Democrat Ro Khanna. As the so-called blue tsunami crashed down, Khanna stopped by Piker’s Twitch stream and said that his colleagues shouldn’t fear Piker’s influence.

“You would think, after this showing around the country, more people would say ‘yeah, you know what, we may not agree with him on everything, but he’s got a huge following,'” Khanna said. “People across the country are resonating with things that he’s saying about the war. Yeah, maybe we should engage.”

Piker does have a huge following, but even the archetypical himbo can’t keep up with a dorky data analyst who loves rolled-up sleeves and bellwether counties. NBC News went all-in on Steve Kornacki and his “Kornacki Cam” during the midterms, and that turned out to be the right move. Kornacki’s breakdown of the blue tsunami collected 29 million views across all platforms to become the #1 election stream. Per Streams Charts, NBC News picked up 4.39 million hours of election night watch time on YouTube.

So while the size of the blue tsunami may have eclipsed predictions, the distribution of electoral coverage was exactly what we expected. Creators have become indispensable political pundits, but there’s still plenty of room at the table for traditional networks, too.

The New York Times is suing the makers of Brave Browser for unauthorized copying of journalism and copyright infringement for allegedly scraping publisher content to sell to AI companies and enabling customers to bypass its paywall. Although Brave positions itself as a white company that benefits consumers, the lawsuit paints a picture of a black hat company that exploits the work of publishers.

Brave Browser and Brave Search positions themselves as the “good guys” on the Internet by casting themselves as the solution to an Internet that’s broken by surveillance capitalism. It positions itself as the antidote to Google’s aggressive monetization of its own users.

The New York Times’ copyright infringement lawsuit against the makers of Brave Browser and Search Engine reveals a darker reality behind the gleaming “user-first” stance in which Brave is alleged to exploit the work of journalists without compensation.

The New York Times lawsuit is a challenge to an alternative business model that instead of exploiting its users the way Google does it exploits the work of publishers on the internet by selling access to that content to AI companies, and uses it to provide answers that compete with the publishers’ own websites.

Brave allegedly provides unauthorized copies of Times journalism through its Search API, allowing third parties to use that content without obtaining licenses from The Times. The content that Brave scrapes off publisher sites is alleged to be sold to AI companies which then can use it to train their large language models. That same content is also sold to be used by AI Chat as grounding content that’s surfaced through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

The complaint cites Brave’s own marketing of its Search API for AI training, grounding, and content extraction as evidence that Brave knowingly promotes uses that The Times considers infringing. This is part of the complaint’s allegation that Brave deliberately created its products to exploit copyrighted content by making it available to third parties, including creating features that bypass publishers’ paywalls.

The inference that can be made here is that if Brave is doing this to The New York Times, it’s likely doing it to other websites that publish content on the Internet, whether it’s a recipe site, a product review site, or any other  kind of website that earns income from showing advertising.

#7497. Are Reddit’s new search ads just an answer engine optimization play?

In a blog post published on November 3, Reddit revealed that it’s testing a new ad product. Alongside a “select group of eligible advertisers,” the social platform is experimenting with paid media posts that show up in its search results.

The new ads will harness Reddit’s “existing ad targeting” to surface relevant product recommendations on search pages. The blog post provided two examples of how that process could work: A search for “espresso station” could show results for coffee machines, beans, and mugs, and a query for “home office equipment” could deliver paid listings for monitors, desks, and chairs.

On their own, the search ads have plenty of utility for brands that want to reach Reddit’s growing community, which includes a large share of Millennial and Gen Z users. At the same time, the new format has intriguing connections to the emerging industry known as answer engine optimization (AEO).

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

AEO is a marketing strategy that uses paid media to affect the referrals made by generative AI models. Reddit was once the king of chatbot referrals; that advantage inspired other platforms to copy its signature layout.

YouTube has since snatched the chatbot referral crown from Reddit, and its ties to AEO strategies are a big reason why. Agencies are working with brands to produce creator content that shows up in future chatbot queries.

Compared to YouTube, Reddit isn’t really a creator hub. Its content is produced by users who typically stay anonymous and stick to text. The type of AEO companies like Zoom are doing on YouTube won’t necessarily work on Reddit.

So as funding continues to pour into the AEO industry, Reddit has to develop its own mechanisms for those marketers. One potential solution is a new video product that resembles TikTok. Those clips can make Reddit more creator-friendly while also retaining control of content that often goes viral on other platforms.

Now, with search ads, Reddit has another solution it can potentially sell to AEO firms. It is letting brands insert themselves on search pages that could be scraped by LLMs. That idea won’t make up the referral gap with YouTube all on its own, but it’s a step in the right direction.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

A Google Lighthouse update changes how PageSpeed Insights simulates page loads, which can raise lab scores on pages that haven't changed.

PageSpeed Insights is now using Lighthouse 13.6.0, which was released Oct. 27. This version of Lighthouse changes how it simulates how long a page takes to load.

Chrome’s Web Performance Developer Advocate, Barry Pollard, has stated on Bluesky that the updated version of PageSpeed Insights with Lighthouse 13.6.0 is now available. He said this improves the simulated FCP (First Contentful Paint) and the simulated LCP (Largest Contentful Paint), both of which Pollard says will be more accurate than before and generally result in higher scores.

A page may receive a different PageSpeed Insights score without anything on it changing, due to the change in the test. Pollard also said that websites heavily dependent on JavaScript would be more likely to see an impact from the updated test.

Pollard quoted a developer who had posted about how single-page apps (SPAs) had seen a big improvement in their results since the Lighthouse update, citing react.dev. He opened his post stating, “True!”, then added:

“Note this is not SPA-specific (and unrelated to other SPA things we’ve been working on), but more likely to impact JS-heavy sites.”

The experimental soft navigation metrics in Chrome that I wrote about back in October are a separate way of measuring user experience. The data comes from real Chrome users through the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) and Lighthouse uses a simulated test.

By default, Lighthouse will load a page at full speed and then estimate how it would load on a slower connection. The throttling docs say that this simulated throttling matches PageSpeed Insights’ setup.

The release notes for version 13.6.0 of Lighthouse list several changes to Lantern, which is the simulation behind those estimates, aimed at improving its accuracy.

Lighthouse 13.5 used each request’s fetch priority to decide whether or not it blocked rendering. In 13.6, Lantern uses Chrome’s own render-blocking label for each request (and falls back to using priority only when that label is missing).

A second change applies when the LCP element is text that appears in the same frame as the page’s first content. Lantern now estimates that LCP from the same requests and page tasks it uses for FCP instead of from a set that can include every request made before LCP.

Ivan Akulov showed in a GitHub issue how the old simulation handled a test page created with Framer whose only content above the fold was text, so one element counted as both FCP and LCP. Lighthouse reported much later LCP than FCP for that text. Even though preloading the page’s JavaScript modules improved interactive time for the real page, they caused simulated LCP to be worse.

Pollard thanked Akulov in a reply, saying he “kicked off some of these improvements.” The Lighthouse team closed the issue as completed in the Lantern upgrade listed in the 13.6 release notes.

Lighthouse 13.6 has also updated the Agentic Resource Discovery (ARD) audit from Lighthouse 13.5, which I covered in September. When Lighthouse 13.5 was released, it looked for an ARD manifest under the old ai-catalog names even though the spec had changed to ard.json. So if your website only used the new name but you didn’t include a line in your robots.txt file called Agentmap, it would show as Not Applicable.

With this update, Lighthouse 13.6 will look for an Agentmap line, a rel="ard" link tag or Link header and /.well-known/ard.json prior to looking for the ai-catalog names. And if Lighthouse 13.6 finds the manifest only at an ai-catalog location, it will note that ARD consumers are not required to check there.

The performance score listed for your page in PageSpeed Insights is based on data generated by Lighthouse. According to Google’s PageSpeed Insights documentation, lab data are results of a simulated load using a single device running on a fixed set of network conditions. They note that “having good lab data does not necessarily mean real-user experiences will also be good.”

Field data (also shown in the same report) represents real visits to your website within the last 28 days, as reported by CrUX. Each PageSpeed Insights report includes the version of Lighthouse used to generate results, next to the emulated device.

PageSpeed Insights scores from before and after the Lighthouse 13.6 update weren’t measured with the same simulation. Part of a higher lab score on a page you just optimized may come from the new version, and charts that track lab scores over time may show a jump at the switch to 13.6.

Before reporting an improvement, check that both reports name the same Lighthouse version, and compare the field data.

Lighthouse’s release notes say its team expects 13.6 to ship in the DevTools of Chrome 159, which is now in Chrome’s desktop Dev channel and in Canary. As of Nov. 2, Chrome’s release schedule lists Chrome 159 for stable release on Dec. 8.

An open issue on Lighthouse’s GitHub is also looking into cases where Lantern’s simulated LCP runs far above measured LCP, using large JavaScript and SPA sites as examples.

#7492. Google Says It’s Okay To Block Some JavaScript Resources With Robots.txt via @sejournal, @martinibuster

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Google's John Mueller clarified whether site owners can use robots.txt to block Googlebot from downloading specific resources that users see.

Google’s John Mueller answered a question about whether it’s okay to block Googlebot from indexing an age-verification popup that website visitors are required to see. His answer offers some clarity about whether it’s okay to purposely hide some kinds of content from Googlebot and explains how site owners can do it.

Google requires publishers to allow Googlebot to crawl everything that a user might see but that wasn’t always the case. There was a time in the early days of SEO where SEOs blocked Google from downloading JavaScript and CSS files in order to optimize the crawl budget and encourage better website indexing.

But there came a time when Google began rendering web pages and subsequently required site owners to allow Googlebot to download all resources that a user would see. Some sites that continued to block Google from downloading critical resources temporarily lost their rankings.

So the question about whether it’s okay to block Google from indexing a popup is reasonable.

The SEO asked on Reddit whether it’s okay to use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from indexing an age-verification popup that a website is legally required to display to visitors.

The person described a hypothetical website that loads an age-verification popup from a separate domain through an API. The question was whether blocking Googlebot from crawling that external domain would prevent the popup from being rendered.

“Say I have a website websiteA.com – for legal reasons it has an age verification pop up that sits on a separate domain and is inserted on the page via an API. Lets call it verificationpopup.com

Lets say I wanted to block Google from seeing this – if I added a disallow on verificationpopup.com/robots.txt would that prevent Google from rendering the pop up?

(this is purley a hypothetical and apologies for the stupid Q, I am not very tech minded)”

Mueller confirmed that using robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from rendering the age-verification popup would generally work. He also suggested an alternative approach that involves blocking a JavaScript file responsible for loading the popup.

“That would generally work. If you’re using a specific JS script file to do this, you could also disallow that specific javascript file via robots.txt. (If you only have one JS file that does a bunch of things, I wouldnt’ do that”

Mueller’s response indicates that Google’s algorithms may be looser than it used to be, at least toward something like this age verification popup. His answer confirmed that site owners can use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from rendering an age-verification popup, even when the popup is displayed to website visitors.

He returned hours later to elaborate in more detail about two ways to accomplish this, addressing two ways the popup is loaded and which resources the site owner can control.

Mueller explained that the first approach involves blocking Googlebot from crawling the external domain that provides the age-verification popup.

In the situation of an external domain that’s the source of the resource that needs blocking, the external domain’s robots.txt can disallow crawling and Googlebot will not fetch those resources and therefore cannot use them to render the popup. Mueller said that this is common with resources related to advertising where a JavaScript file responsible for showing ads is blocked by robots.txt.

the embedded site’s content is blocked by robots.txt. If you embed content from verificationpopup-com on your site (say via iframe or by calling a script on verificationpopup-com, etc), and verificationpopup-com disallows all crawling, then crawlers that follow robots.txt (like Googlebot) would not fetch that content, and would not use it in rendering.

This is how many ads services work. Googlebot wouldn’t crawl these URLs like a separate page, but it would try to fetch them during the course of rendering, and if robots.txt blocks it, then it doesn’t fetch the content, and can’t use it. You need to make sure that your pages still load when those URLs are not fetched, but for something like this, that’s usually not a problem.

Your site uses a specific JS file to load this, and you block that yourself. For example, perhaps you use a “load-verification-popup.js” file to do this. If you block that page with robots.txt on your site, then the script won’t be loaded during rendering (blocked by robots.txt).

In my experience, this is less common, but it’s an option. If the robots.txt on verificationpopup-com is not something you can influence, you’d need to do this, if you wanted to prevent it from being visible/used during rendering.”

So to recap, the second approach involves blocking a JavaScript file that’s used to load the popup that’s on another domain where using a robots.txt is not an option.

The interesting part of Mueller’s answer is that he confirmed a way to deliberately prevent Googlebot from rendering an age-verification popup that human visitors are required to see.

He also explained that the website must continue to load properly when Googlebot cannot fetch the blocked resources. For an age-verification popup like the one described in the question, he indicated that this is usually not a problem.

The overall takeaway is that it’s okay to use robots.txt to prevent Googlebot from downloading and rendering an age-verification popup, even though human visitors are required to see it. Mueller’s answer shows that website owners exercise some control over which resources Googlebot uses during rendering, including resources that are a part of the experience presented to visitors.

RELATED ARTICLEIn Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than everSophie CulpepperOctober 22, 2025If you thought last year was bleak, Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder.

What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin, founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.”

In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged.

Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report.

“When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states.

RELATED ARTICLELast year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s goingSophie CulpepperFebruary 9, 2026Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024.

“Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois. “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.”

The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left.

A few other highlights from this year’s report:

The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas.

Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022.

Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit. The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms.

The most important stories about journalism and the future of news, delivered to your inbox every afternoon.

The unrestricted funding helped small outlets plug holes and try new things, but publishers ran up against the limits of what two $50,000 grants could accomplish, especially when it came to hiring.

#7489. When Slate went back to its 1996 homepage, it learned some web design lessons for 2026

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate, now 20 years old, reflects on the value of taking the long view and not chasing digital media trendsShan WangSeptember 23, 2016The fonts are Times New Roman and Arial Narrow, the colors are maroon and mustard, and the cursor is the 8-bit pixel hand. When Slate revived its original 1996 homepage to celebrate its 30th birthday this fall1, the team found a lot to like besides nostalgia.

“I’ve read Slate since 1997, when I finally had access to my own computer at my first job,” Hillary Frey, Slate’s editor-in-chief, told me recently. At the age of 51, she said, “I’m speaking as an old. But I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

Slate’s homepage has long functioned as a “fossil of what the internet was during that time,” said Ivylise Simones, Slate’s creative director. In 1996, Slate was trying to figure out what a magazine on the internet should even look like; in 2026, it’s among the last general-interest digital-native news sites, and print magazines are dying out. “Salon is one of our only lasting contemporaries,” Frey noted. “There are other sort of fellows from that era, like Feed and Nerve. They’ve been gone for awhile.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate launches a metered paywall to draw more membership revenue from readers, not just listenersSarah ScireMarch 26, 2020In its 30th anniversary campaign, Slate has found its fossil-like nature to be something of a selling point. (It can also be a challenge.) Over the years, the site has published a number of posts about its history and editorial and design choices. A decade ago, then–news editor Chad Lorenz wrote “A history of Slate in nine home pages.” (At launch, Slate articles included page numbers and printing instructions.) A 1998 paywall, Lorenz wrote, was “fortunately” abandoned by 1999. But the paywall returned in 2020. (It was metered at the start, but today it’s dynamic, changing based on user behavior.) For its 30th birthday, the site is running a promotion: a year of access for $19.96.

RELATED ARTICLECan’t read just one: Slate’s daily advice columns are strange, funny, deep, and increasingly a major traffic driver for the siteLaura Hazard OwenJuly 22, 2019“Going back to our roots, there are certain elements we are starting to really love,” Simones said, and she’s thinking about how to include them in the site’s ongoing redesign. She likes the spareness and simplicity of earlier versions of the site, she said, pointing to Reddit and Discord as places that are “more reminiscent of old homepages than the current, very stylized, very gridded layout” found across the internet. A less dense homepage on desktop, she said, is “refreshing.”

“Our editorial guiding light is the mix,” Frey added. Slate has verticals, but they’re not emphasized in the story selection at the top of the homepage; instead, life, politics, and advice stories are mixed together and weighted similarly. “Having an image for every story you share on the homepage is just not necessary,” Simones noted.

Some 1990s-era headline styles still work, too, Frey has found. One of her favorites is a 2002 piece by Slate founding editor Michael Kinsley: “The secret vice of power women.”

“He was writing it about his wife, who found tremendous satisfaction and relaxation in watching police procedurals,” Frey said. “That’s something I still identify with, though most of them now are from Finland and Norway. 100%, this headline would play on the Slate homepage right this second.”

Art courtesy of Slate A wrinkle for 2026: The 1996-inspired homepage had to work on mobile, even though nobody was reading Slate on a phone 30 years ago. [↩]

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

Scale a global AI content factory with approved local facts and human expertise to help AI search reflect each market's products, rules, and customers.

For more than 25 years, I have heard the same complaints from local marketing teams. “This doesn’t sound like us.” “Our customers don’t ask that question.” “That product isn’t even sold here.” “Why are we publishing a U.S. case study on the Japanese site?”

At headquarters, these complaints were usually treated as resistance. Local teams simply wanted control, and they didn’t understand the cost of supporting 30 or 40 markets. They were slowing down a process that had been carefully engineered for speed and consistency.

I understood that view. I also spent a lot of time explaining the local side of the argument to global teams who weren’t necessarily happy to hear it.

Now AI is giving enterprises the ability to produce content for every market faster and more cheaply than ever. And AI search is showing us, very clearly, what happens when that content is the same everywhere.

The local teams may have been right all along.

This article examines why the traditional global content model is breaking down in AI search, and how to build an AI-powered content factory that scales without erasing what makes each market unique.

Most multinational content operations were designed to solve one problem: how to publish the same message in many languages without the cost growing at the same rate as the number of markets.

The industry developed very good tools for that problem:

The key performance indicators followed the same logic: cost per word, TM leverage, reducing turnaround time, and accelerating time-to-market for a global launch. A high TM match rate was the key to maximizing KPIs and building confidence in uniform messaging.

When local teams pushed back, the rationale for pushback was hard to quantify. It was typically framed in terms of tone, nuance, or lack of cultural fit. When matched against a dashboard of cost savings, “it doesn’t feel local” rarely won the argument.

In traditional search, the cost of that decision was manageable. Hreflang told search engines which language and country version to show, so a translated page could still rank in its market. If the page was thin, it usually ranked a little lower. It didn’t disappear.

See also: Lost In Translation: How Language Changes Which Brand AI Recommends

AI search changes the unit of competition. Traditional search selected a page. AI search builds an answer from facts, passages, and evidence collected from many sources. That shift exposes a significant problem the traditional efficiency model created.

When search engines find a cluster of pages that are essentially the same, they don’t fully process and store every version. One version is selected as the canonical and processed in full. The others are treated more like alternate names that point back to it, carrying only enough information (URL, language, country) to be served in the right context.

AI systems refer to this as canonical tokenization, the process by which text across different languages is split, compressed, and processed. It is efficient for the search engine, and it works reasonably well when the job is to swap one URL for another on a results page.

It works much less well when an AI system is retrieving passages to build an answer. The passage it retrieves often comes from the canonical version, and once that passage is pulled out of the page, it no longer carries the URL that told everyone which market it belonged to.

I described the result in How AI’s Geo-Identification Failures Are Rewriting International SEO: When markets look the same, the strongest instance of your content wins. In most global companies, that is the U.S. or main English site.

So a buyer in Germany may get U.S. product availability. A patient in Japan may read about a product or use that is not approved there. A Spanish-language query from Spain may be answered with content written for Mexico.

This is the uncomfortable part for those of us who built global content programs. Translation memory was designed to maximize content reuse at scale. AI retrieval systems are designed to discard reuse.

Every sentence we reused across 30 markets now makes those markets look more alike to a machine. The higher our TM leverage, the stronger the case that our local pages were alternate versions of one global page, not unique sources worth retrieving in their own right.

When local teams said “this doesn’t feel like our market,” they were describing exactly what an AI system now concludes.

The twin engines of the marketing agility framework describe two forces every multinational has to run at the same time:

Research on the framework found that organizations perform best when both engines are running. Most global content programs, however, were built almost entirely around the global engine. The local engine was treated as a cost to be minimized, because local responsiveness was expensive. Every market-specific page needed a writer, a reviewer, and a budget line.

The usual way enterprises use AI today is to make the global engine faster: translate more content into more languages with fewer people. That produces more of the same near-identical pages, only quicker. It is a faster photocopier.

The bigger opportunity is to use AI to make the local engine more affordable. If AI handles the tedious and time-consuming activities of drafting, translation, structuring, and formatting, people in each market can spend their time on what only they can provide: local evidence, local questions, and local judgment.

A content factory built for AI search starts from a different premise. The product isn’t pages. The product is governed, market-scoped knowledge, and pages are one of the ways that knowledge is published.

Before anything is written or translated, the organization needs a single source of truth where its important claims live. Each fact should record:

This sounds like a governance exercise, and it is. It is also the only reliable way to prevent a fact that is true in one market from being published or retrieved as if it were true in all of them.

This is the most important change to the translation workflow. Not every sentence should be treated the same way.

Translation memory is still valuable for the first category. Product names, for example, should be identical across languages so that AI systems recognize them as the same entity. It is, however, a mistake to let TM leverage fill the second category. When a market-variable slot is empty, the factory should flag it, not copy the U.S. version into it.

With the fact registry and the segment rules in place, AI can now handle most of the production work by drafting from approved facts, translating and structuring pages around real questions, and verifying that the right source has been integrated for every market-variable slot.

This is where the cost savings come from now. The savings don’t come from reusing more sentences. They come from automating everything related to local evidence, so local teams can supply that evidence without bearing the full cost of producing the page.

The global engine contributes what should be identical everywhere; the local engine contributes what must differ. Both meet in the fact registry, and AI assembles each market’s pages from it.

“Keeping the human touch” is often understood as keeping a human post-editor at the end of the machine translation process. That role is becoming harder to defend on quality alone. A recent localization benchmark published here on Search Engine Journal found AI workflows outscored human translators in four of six content types.

I don’t read that as the end of human involvement. I read it as a signal that the human value has moved upstream.

In an AI content factory, people in each market are needed at four points:

Notice that these are the same things local teams were complaining about for years. They were never really asking for better translation. They were asking for their market’s reality to be represented.

This also changes how global SEO and content teams should be organized. The roles and service-level agreements I described in Effective SEO Organizational Structure For A Global Company need to include ownership of local evidence, not only local publishing.

Because AI systems retrieve passages that lose their URL context, each important passage has to carry its own market information. A few simple rules make a large difference:

These rules are easy to build into an AI-assisted workflow. They are much harder to apply consistently when 40 vendors are translating by hand.

Most global teams can tell you how many pages they published per market. Very few can tell you what an AI assistant says about them in each market.

That measurement should be part of the factory, not a one-time audit. Build a fixed set of priority prompts for each market, in the local language, and run them across the major AI assistants on a regular schedule. Then track four things:

Market leakage is the metric I’d watch most closely. It is the most direct measure of whether your local content is being recognized as local. It also gives local teams something they never had in the old model: evidence that their concerns are affecting the business.

Test in local languages, not just English. An English-only visibility check will not show you what a buyer in Seoul or Madrid is seeing.

Consider a composite example drawn from patterns common to global medical device manufacturers.

The company has a well-run global site with a dozen market versions. The technical setup, by traditional international SEO standards, is mostly correct, including hreflang and localized URLs. By traditional international SEO standards, it passes.

When viewed for geographical signals market by market, the picture is completely different:

None of these are translation problems. Each one is a missing piece of local knowledge, and each one was probably raised by someone in that market at some point.

The fix follows the factory model: Register the facts by market, mark which content is market-variable, have local teams supply the evidence and the questions, let AI assemble and structure the pages, and measure what AI assistants say in each language afterward.

The global content model wasn’t wrong to pursue efficiency. For a long time, local responsiveness at scale was simply too expensive, and search engines, using hreflang, were forgiving enough that translated pages could still compete.

AI search removes that forgiveness. When content is the same or very similar everywhere, AI systems collapse them into a single entity, and the strongest version speaks for every market.

AI also removes the excuse. The work that made local content expensive (drafting, translating, formatting, structuring) is exactly the work AI does well. What remains for people is the work local teams were asking to do all along.

So before you scale your content factory with AI, ask a simple question: Are you using AI to publish more of the same, faster? Or are you using it to give each market what it was asking for, finally?

#7486. Two creators went to NYU’s business school, then decided to make a show about the news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“Our videos are what we wish we could consume more of.”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

On a September afternoon in Manhattan’s Union Square neighborhood, Shreyas Sinha is sitting on a toilet, wearing a blue suit. Looking into the camera, he asks, “Why is it that everything I’ve been eating this year is giving me diarrhea?”

Sinha is about to link the 2026 cyclospora outbreaks to decades of problems at the Food and Drug Administration. “I’m only allowed to make three diarrhea jokes in this video,” Sinha says. “I live in tyranny.”

The toilet video is one of the tamer stunts that Sinha and his co-creator, Gaurav Srivatchan, have pulled for their YouTube channel, A Show About The News, a weekly deep dive into major business and politics stories (tagline: “Critics are calling it the worst alternative to mainstream media, and those are just the critics I’m related to.”)

In a video about why young people can’t afford to buy homes, Sinha pops out of a cardboard box on the street and takes former New York City mayor Eric Adams to a studio apartment filled with men. Other recent videos include a 45-minute interview on the street with former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci, an explainer on prediction market ads, and a rap music video on why retirement investments are safer than get-rich-quick schemes.

Sinha, 25, and Srivatchan, 22, met in 2023 when they were students at New York University’s Stern School of Business. They teamed up to make short vertical explainer videos, but those didn’t take off as much as they’d hoped. In 2024, Sinha quit his finance job to pursue A Show About The News full-time, and they transitioned to creating long-form deep dives with a dash of their own humor.

I chatted with Sinha and Srivatchan about how they launched their media careers, how they use humor to explain the news, and what they think business opportunities are for creators today. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Tameez: Why did you start creating news videos? Sinha: Gaurav and I started making videos together during the spring 2023 semester, when I was a senior at NYU and he was a freshman. I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. It seemed like everything was [pointing to], “Hey, you should start making short-form videos.” And then Gaurav was like, “Hey, I’m actually really good at editing videos.” We were not really thinking of it as a YouTube channel, but as making short-form stories. At the time, we were called Fifty50 Media. We were all about trying to distill the world into bipartisan perspectives. We eventually started focusing more on deeper-dive stories. We renamed ourselves to A Show About the News. It’s very easy to put out a political opinion that goes viral, but we really wanted to focus on good stories. Eventually, we started making videos for Morning Brew, and we joined Morning Brew full-time as a franchise in August 2025.

I had been doing a newsletter for a while, I had been doing stand-up comedy for a few years, and I was interning at CNN. Srivatchan: We realized that building a loyal audience off shorts wasn’t feasible in the long-term. And we constantly [faced] the challenge of bringing in nuance. That’s one of the reasons we started working on long-form videos. We try to bring in the political economy lens from our college education and highlight the underlying principles [of] today’s headlines. Sinha: To be honest, we weren’t successful in short-form. We had made 50 or 60 shorts… Srivatchan: Some of them would pop off, get a million views. But the way people consume on the internet is very different from the way people consume when they go to a theater, [where] they’re paying for an experience and they’re going to watch a specific thing. YouTube and social media are like a theater where you can leave and go watch another movie at any time. That’s the challenge of making videos on the internet.

Sinha: After our first video that got a million views, we were like, “Oh shit, this is it.” And it wasn’t. We added followers, but it wasn’t like we were going to get 100,000 people to come back in the next short. We were competing against the new Frozen movie and The Office and Mr. Beast exploding dynamite in his backyard. Tameez: Tell me more about how the Morning Brew deal happened. Srivatchan: I was in London, studying abroad. I slapped a bunch of logos as watermarks on our old videos [and sent them as] demo reels to news outlets. We made another and another, and then they were like, “You guys should just do this for us.” Srivatchan: Morning Brew provided us access to this office. We’re not going into meetings asking, can we do this topic next week? It’s a very high-trust environment, which, from talking to other people who work at other media companies, is extremely rare. We’re not going into meetings asking, can we do this topic next week? It’s a very high-trust environment, which, from talking to other people who work at other media companies, is extremely rare. Tameez: You guys both left careers in finance to do this full-time. Sinha: It was an economically stupid decision, but I knew that if I failed now, I would be young enough to start again. It’s easy to have the golden handcuffs of waiting until the right time, but there is never a right time. It was taking a bet on myself and someone who I really trusted. Still, our videos were getting 12 views at that time; it wasn’t as if something took off and it was like, “Okay, this can pay our bills.”

Srivatchan: I had the advantage of being younger. [Shreyas left] a full-time job. I did my summer internship in consulting and got my return offer, but it was a lot less of a risk for me, personally. It obviously helped that we had some backing from Morning Brew. Tameez: Why is making A Show About the News important now? How does it fit into the larger information ecosystem? Sinha: What we do, in the context of where we went to school, is the equivalent of becoming ballerinas. All of my friends are investment bankers in private equity or in consulting. That is the tried and true method [for NYU Stern graduates]. If you tell people, “Hey, I’m not recruiting for banking, I’m thinking of doing consulting,” they look at you like you just said you want to be an art major. When we said we were going to build a media company, it was truly mind-boggling for people. I loved what Fareed Zakaria did, what Ezra Klein did, but my favorite people when I was a kid were Jon Stewart and John Oliver, Hasan Minhaj and Seth Meyers and Conan O’Brien and Nathan Fielder. I knew I wasn’t going to be a great stand-up comedian, I wasn’t going to be a great writer, but maybe I could combine those to make a job out of it. It’s easy to pat ourselves on the back and say there’s a lot of garbage out there. But also, it has never been a better time to be an independent creator. If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

If we both wanted to go into media today, we would be grabbing water for hosts who get paid $60 million a year. Instead, we actually get to put our own ideas out there.

Tameez: Tell me about your workflow, from video ideation to posting. Sinha: We don’t do short-form clips [from longer videos]. We script our shorts. That takes a ton of time. [But] long-form is the priority. It takes much more time, but you really get to have a relationship with the audience. Srivatchan: When it comes to shorts, either Shreyas or I will have something that really interests us for the week. We start scripting it, then we switch the scripts and each of us does a pass on the other’s. Then we revise them and film them. That takes roughly two out of five workdays. We spend the rest of the time on long-form. We’re also doing a weekly livestream to discuss the headlines with the audience and build that audience connection. So our output is two native short-form, one long-form, and one live stream per week.
